text:
When vehicles cross a suspension bridge, or even when the structure stands empty under its own weight, every pound of force must ultimately find a safe path into the earth. A suspension bridge accomplishes this through a carefully orchestrated interplay of tension and compression, routing loads upward before sending them down into the ground. The journey begins at the deck, the flat roadway carrying traffic and enduring wind. Most suspension bridge decks are reinforced by a stiffening truss or an aerodynamic box girder beneath or around the roadway. Rather than allowing a passing truck to bend one isolated section of road, this rigid deck structure spreads the localized weight across a broader span and resists twisting or fluttering in high winds.

Instead of resting directly on pillars beneath the water or gorge, the deck hangs in the air from a series of vertical steel ropes called suspenders or hangers. Attached at regular intervals along the edges of the deck, these suspenders are pulled taut by gravity acting on the roadway below. Every suspender operates purely in tension, acting like a vertical tether that holds up its assigned section of the deck while pulling downward on the sweeping main cables draped high above.

The main cables are the defining silhouette and the primary workhorses of the bridge. Anchored at both ends of the crossing and draped over tall towers, these thick bundles of thousands of spun steel wires hang in a natural curve that adjusts into a parabolic shape once the uniform weight of the deck is suspended from them. As the suspenders tug downward at dozens of points along the span, the main cables absorb these vertical loads and translate them into enormous internal tension running along the length of the steel strands toward the towers and the shore.

At the top of each towering pylon, the main cables rest in heavy steel grooves called saddles. Because the cables slope downward on either side of the tower, the combined pull of the cables on the main span and the side spans presses straight down onto the saddles. Their opposing horizontal pulls largely balance one another out, transforming the diagonal tension of the cables into massive vertical compression inside the towers. Built from steel or reinforced concrete, the towers act like giant columns, channeling this tremendous downward squeeze straight through their legs and into deep foundations, caissons, or piers resting firmly on bedrock beneath the riverbed or valley floor.

Yet the towers alone cannot hold up the bridge; if the main cables were not tied down at their ends, their tension would pull the towers inward and collapse the entire span. That vital resistance is provided by the anchorages at each end of the bridge. As the main cables descend from the towers toward the ground, they splay out into individual strands secured to giant steel eyebars embedded inside colossal blocks of concrete or pinned directly into solid rock cliffs. The sheer mass and friction of these anchorages resist the relentless horizontal and upward tug of the main cables, locking the tension safely into the earth and completing the load path from the roadway to the ground.
